## Setup repository.

Once you have git installed, or are using some other terminal emulator it is
time to make your first repo.

First, change directory into where ever you would like to keep your project
folder. 

For the purpose of consistency I will use the `~/Documents` folder.

`cd ~/Documents`

Now, create a project directory:

`mkdir ./example_project`

Then change directories into it:

`cd ./example_project`

Then lets initaliaze a new git repository:

`git init`

Then lets list all of files within the current directory:

`ls -a`

You will see that a new directory: `.git/` was created. This is what makes a
directory a git repository. This `.git/` directory is where `git` keeps track of
everything it needs to provide you will all of its functionality.

## Configuration

There is a set of commands to configure git through the command line, we will
start with some basic configuration.

Git comes with configuration on both the global (across repos) and the repo
level. Although, most of the time you will just use the global configuration.


Check to see if your username and email are set:

- `git config --get user.name`
- `git config --get user.email`

If they are not set, then I reccomend that you change them to your Github
username, and email.

- `git config --add --global user.name "github_username_here"`
- `git config --add --global user.emil "email@something.com"`

It is also good practice to set your default branch:

`git config --add --global init.defaultBranch main`

It is good to know that when we are configuring git using these commands, git is
just changing some files for us.

Global configs are stored in `~/.gitconfig`

Local configs are stored in `./.git/config`

## Baiscs

The main functionality of git is that you get to save your work. Git is powerful
because the user has full control over how they choose to save. There are a few
states that git may view a file to be in.

Try running `git status` in your new project repository.

This command shows us the current status of our repsitory, it will show you
which files are untracked, staged, and commited.

- `untracked` - Git will not track this file.
- `staged` - Marked for inculsion in the next commit.
- `commited` - Saved to the repositories history.

`git status` is very useful to uderstand the current state of your repository,
so that you could decide what to do next. We will use it often in this workshop.

### First Commit

Now lets learn how to save our work.

Make sure that you are in the root of you project directory:

`pwd` - Print working directory.

Now lets make create a new file:

If you are familiar with a terminal based text editor like vim or nano, I
encourage you to use it here. If not, open this file with your favorite text
editor.

Create a new file: `hello.md`

Then write "hello world!" into the file and save it, and head back to our
teminal instnace.

Run: `git status`

You will see that the new file "hello.md" that we just created is untracked.

We would like to keep track of "hello.md" so lets run:

`git add hello.md`

Now, check the status again:

`git status`

You will see that "hello.md" is now a staged file.

Git does not store entire files, nor does it store the difference between
changed files. It is more acurate to view a commit as a picture, or a
screenshot of your project directory at the time of your commit. 

`git commit -m "Add hello.md"`

The `git commit` command will save a snapshot of the staged files, the argument
`-m` means that the preceding text within the quotation marks will be the commit
message. Our commit message should be short and informative.

## Internals

Now that we have learned how to save or work, lets learn how git actually keeps
track of everything. Understanding a little about the internals of git will help
you to understand some best practices and work-flow a bit better. It is also
interesting!

We can view our commit history using the command:

`git log`

`git log` is very useful in understanding the structures of your commits, we
will use it often in this wokrshop.

Currently, we only have a single commit. Which should look something like this:

```
commit b556efb1dcb4bdbfd971b615e8dae4cd26882f91 (HEAD -> master)
Author: mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com>
Date:   Sun Feb 15 16:14:11 2026 -0500

    Add hello.md
```

We can learn a lot about how git works through investigating this `commit` line.

This string of seemingly random characters is a hash. It is how git efficiently
stores and identifies everything it needs to manage your project. 

Git provides a very useful inspecting these hashes:

`git cat-file -p YOUR_COMMIT_HASH_HERE`

**NOTE: You only need to provide the first 4 characters of the hash, so no
need to type it all out.**

Git tells us exactly what information is provided by the commit hash:

```
tree 9155d858058637fd4552c960d7f11546e579850b
author mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com> 1771190051 -0500
committer mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com> 1771190051 -0500

Add hello.md
```

We see another hash, this time it is a tree hash. This is gits way of storing
your project directory.

We could then cat out this as well.

`git cat-file -p YOUR_TREE_HASH_HERE`

This is the result:

```
100644 blob a0423896973644771497bdc03eb99d5281615b51    hello.md
```

Now we can see a blob hash, this is how files are tracked using git. We can see
the `hello.md` the file that we commited.

We can once again see what this hash means to git.

`git cat-file -p YOUR_BLOB_HASH_HERE`

This is the result:

```
hello world!
```

It's the contents of our commited file!

In summary, git uses three types of objects, each identified by a hash:

| Object | What it stores |
|---|---|
| Commit | Metadata (author, date, message) and a pointer to a tree. |
| Tree | A snapshot of your project directory, containing pointers to blobs. |
| Blob | The raw contents of a single file. |


```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Commit["Commit<br/>b556ef...<br/>Add hello.md"]
    Tree["Tree<br/>9155d8..."]
    Blob["Blob<br/>a04238...<br/>(hello.md)"]

    Commit --> Tree
    Tree --> Blob
```

Now lets make another commit:

First create a new file using your text editor or IDE.

Call this file "contents.md"

Within this file, type: "contents" save it.

Then back in your terminal:

`git add contents.md` to mark the file as staged.

`git commit -m "Added contents"` to commit the file to your history.

Now run `git --no-pager log --oneline --parents` to view our commit history in a
more compact way.

```
f700dd5 b556efb (HEAD -> master) added contents
b556efb Add hello.md
```

Our second commit has two hashes next to it, the first hash is its own, the
second is its parent. Our orginal commit had no parents, since it was the first.


we can investigate our new commits hash:

`git cat-file -p YOUR_COMMIT_HASH_HERE`

```
tree f9d01e625a573fa544c00a0d4acf98c985006c71
parent b556efb1dcb4bdbfd971b615e8dae4cd26882f91
author mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com> 1772047353 -0500
committer mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com> 1772047353 -0500

added contents
```

Notice that the tree hash is differnt then the the tree hash of our first
commit.

lets investigate it:

`git cat-file -p YOUR_TREE_HASH_HERE`

```
100644 blob 12f00e90b6ef79117ce6e650416b8cf517099b78    contents.md
100644 blob a0423896973644771497bdc03eb99d5281615b51    hello.md
```

Notice that, since we never changed hello.md, the hash remains the same.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    CommitA["Commit<br/>b556ef...<br/>Add hello.md"]
    CommitB["Commit<br/>f700dd...<br/>Added contents"]
    TreeA["Tree<br/>9155d8..."]
    TreeB["Tree<br/>f9d01e..."]
    BlobHello["Blob<br/>a04238...<br/>(hello.md)"]
    BlobContents["Blob<br/>12f00e...<br/>(contents.md)"]

    CommitB --> CommitA
    CommitA --> TreeA
    CommitB --> TreeB
    TreeA --> BlobHello
    TreeB --> BlobContents
    TreeB --> BlobHello
```

Each commit points to its own tree, which represents the state of your project
at that moment in time. But since hello.md was unchanged, both trees point to
the exact same blob.

This is why git is so efficient even on large projects with long histories. Only
the files that actually changed take up new space.

## Branching

Now that we understand some of the inner workings of git, we can learn more
about functionality. One of the most useful features in git is the ability to
branch off of you current commit line. Branching allows you to take the project in a
new direction, while preserving the original project entirely.

PUT IN AN DIAGRAM EXAMPLE HERE

Branching is also necessary to understand if you are working on a collabrative
project with multiple people. 

We can list all of the branches in our repo with:

`git branch`

Currently we only have our default branch: `main` which we set the name of
earlier.

Create a new branch:

`git branch test`

Where `test` is the name of the branch that we are creating.

`git switch test` will then allow us to switch to a specified branch. 

Lets make a commit on this branch.

Create a new file `groceries.md`, within the file add:

```
Eggs
Cheese
Milk
```

back in the terminal: 

`git add groceries.md`

`git commit -m "added grocery list"`

we can again look at the commit history:

`git log`

You can see that all of our previous commits to `main` are listed here, in
addtion the commit that we have just made is also listed. 

now lets switch back to `main`

git switch `main`

now use `git log` again to compare the commit history between branches.

You will see that the commit that we made to `test` is missing. 

Now, this is the functionality of branches, our `test` branch will preserve the
history and changes up to the time the new branch is created. Any changes on
one branch will have no effect on other branches. This allows you to take a
project in a new direction, without effecting the original project.

Lets create another commit on `main`

Double check that you are still on the main branch `git branch`

Create a new file: `movies.md`

and within the file add:

```
The God Father
The Dark Night
Back To The Future
```

Now, add and commit this file be sure that you are on `main` and use the commit
message "added movies.md".

now run: `git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

The argument `--decorate` will allow us to see the commit history across
branches. The rest of the arguments are there for convience. 

You could see that these most recent commits share the same parent. This is the
point of divergence and illustrates how branches represent a new commit history
at a chosen point.

## Merge

Imagine you are using git to manage the creation of a Website. Imagine that you
have created a new branch to test some differnt colors for the background of
this website. Now lets say that you like how these changes look, and want the
main branch to incorperate the changes. There are a few ways to do this, the
most simple way would be to merege the branches. 


Lets merge our branches to demostrate what this may look like:

Double check that you are on the correct branch. When merging branches, you
should be sure that you are on the brach that you would like to incorperate the
changes onto. For us, that is `main`.

then use `git merge test`

where `test` is the branch to merge.

## Revert

To illustrate why this is so powerful, think about the back button in your
browser. Your browser keeps track of the pages you visit as a kind of history
tree. If you hit the back button and then click a new link, you lose your
ability to go "forward" to where you were that branch.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
		A["google.com"]
		B["wikipedia.org"]
		C["wikipedia.org/git"]
		D["wikipedia.org/linux"]

		A --> B --> C
		B --> D
```

In this example, if you navigated to wikipedia.org/git and then hit back and
clicked through to wikipedia.org/linux, there is no built-in way to get back to
wikipedia.org/git. It is simply lost.

Git gives you full control so that this never has to happen to your code. You
can move freely between any point in your commit history, create new branches
from any commit, and never worry about losing work.
